Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 10 of 10): Winds of Change to the Last Flag, 1960–1997 and After

Summary: Between 1960 and 1984 more than thirty British colonies became independent, mostly in Africa, the Caribbean, the Gulf and the Pacific. It was not always peaceful: Aden, Konfrontasi, Dhofar, Rhodesia, the Chagos expulsions and the Falklands all came in this period. The handover of Hong Kong in 1997 is usually treated as the end of the empire. This final post covers 1960 to 1997, then what happened afterwards, and ends with a single table pulling the whole series together.

---

## The big picture

In February 1960 Prime Minister Harold Macmillan told the South African parliament in Cape Town that "the wind of change is blowing through this continent". Within a decade almost all of British Africa was independent. The pace surprised even the officials carrying it out.

Several pressures came together: the cost of counter-insurgency after Kenya and Cyprus, the humiliation of Suez, pressure from the US and the UN, the strength of nationalist movements, and a British economy shifting toward Europe. In 1968 the Labour government announced that Britain would withdraw its forces from "East of Suez" by 1971.

The settler colonies were the hardest cases. In Rhodesia, the white minority declared independence on its own terms in 1965 rather than accept majority rule, starting a war that lasted until 1979.

## Independence by year

| Year | Countries that became independent from Britain (or left British protection) |
|---|---|
| 1960 | Somaliland (June, then joined Somalia), Cyprus (August), Nigeria (October) |
| 1961 | Kuwait (June), Sierra Leone (April), Tanganyika (December); South Cameroons joins Cameroon after a plebiscite |
| 1962 | Jamaica (August), Trinidad and Tobago (August), Uganda (October) |
| 1963 | Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore join Malaysia (September); Zanzibar (December); **Kenya** (12 December) |
| 1964 | Malawi (July), Malta (September), Zambia (October) |
| 1965 | The Gambia (February), Maldives (July); Rhodesia's illegal UDI (November) |
| 1966 | Guyana (May), Botswana (September), Lesotho (October), Barbados (November) |
| 1967 | South Yemen (Aden), 30 November |
| 1968 | Mauritius (March), Swaziland, now Eswatini (September) |
| 1970 | Tonga (end of protected status), Fiji (October) |
| 1971 | Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (end of the Trucial and protected-state treaties) |
| 1973 | The Bahamas |
| 1974 | Grenada |
| 1976 | Seychelles |
| 1978 | Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, Dominica |
| 1979 | St Lucia, Kiribati, St Vincent and the Grenadines |
| 1980 | **Zimbabwe** (April), Vanuatu (from the Anglo-French condominium) |
| 1981 | Belize, Antigua and Barbuda |
| 1983 | St Kitts and Nevis |
| 1984 | Brunei (1 January) |
| 1997 | **Hong Kong** returned to China (1 July) |

## Main timeline (1960–1997)

| Date | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| February 1960 | Macmillan's "wind of change" speech in Cape Town | |
| March 1960 | Sharpeville massacre in South Africa (69 killed) | |
| May 1961 | South Africa becomes a republic and leaves the Commonwealth | Rejoined in 1994 |
| July 1961 | Operation Vantage: British troops sent to Kuwait against an Iraqi threat | |
| 1962 | Commonwealth Immigrants Act restricts migration from the colonies and Commonwealth; West Indies Federation dissolves | |
| December 1962 | **Brunei Revolt** | Leads into Konfrontasi |
| 1963–1966 | **Konfrontasi**: Indonesia fights Malaysia in Borneo; British and Commonwealth troops defend Malaysia | |
| 1963–1967 | **Aden Emergency** | Ends with a chaotic British withdrawal |
| 1963–1976 | **Dhofar Rebellion** in Oman, with British officers and the SAS supporting the Sultan | |
| January 1964 | Zanzibar Revolution; army mutinies in Tanganyika, Uganda and Kenya put down with British help | |
| August 1965 | Singapore leaves Malaysia | |
| November 1965 | **Rhodesia's UDI**; British Indian Ocean Territory created by detaching the Chagos Islands from Mauritius | |
| 1967–1970 | Nigerian Civil War (Biafra) | Britain supplies arms to the Nigerian federal government |
| 1968–1973 | **Expulsion of the Chagossians** so that Diego Garcia can become a US military base | About 1,500 to 2,000 people removed |
| January 1968 | Britain announces withdrawal "East of Suez" | |
| 1968 | Commonwealth Immigrants Act (1968) aimed at Kenyan Asians; Enoch Powell's "Rivers of Blood" speech | |
| 1969 | Operation Sheepskin: British paratroopers land on Anguilla after it breaks away from St Kitts | One of the last British "invasions" of a colony, and a peaceful one |
| August 1969 | British troops deployed in Northern Ireland; the **Troubles** (c.1968–1998) | |
| 1971 | British forces withdraw from the Gulf and Singapore | |
| January 1972 | **Bloody Sunday** in Derry: 13 killed by British soldiers, another later dies | |
| 1972 | Ceylon becomes the republic of Sri Lanka; Idi Amin expels Uganda's Asians, about 28,000 come to Britain | |
| January 1973 | UK joins the European Economic Community | |
| 1974 | Turkish invasion of Cyprus; Britain keeps its Sovereign Base Areas | |
| 1972–1979 | **Rhodesian Bush War** (the Second Chimurenga) | Around 30,000 killed |
| December 1979 | Lancaster House Agreement | Leads to Zimbabwe's independence in 1980 |
| 1981 | British Nationality Act creates separate citizenships | Many people in the remaining territories lose their right to live in Britain |
| April–June 1982 | **Falklands War** | 255 British and 649 Argentine military dead, and three islanders |
| 1982 | Canada Act "patriates" Canada's constitution | |
| December 1984 | **Sino-British Joint Declaration** on Hong Kong | |
| 1986 | Australia Act ends the last legal links between the Australian states and the UK parliament | |
| 1989 | Tiananmen Square crackdown; Berlin Wall falls | Increases Hong Kong's anxiety about 1997 |
| 1990–1994 | Mandela released; first democratic elections in South Africa | |
| 30 June to 1 July 1997 | **Hong Kong handover**; the last Governor, Chris Patten, leaves on the royal yacht *Britannia* | Usually seen as the symbolic end of the empire |

## Resistance and conflict in the final decades

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1962 | North Kalimantan National Army (TNKU) | Brunei | Suppressed |
| 1963–1966 | Indonesia | Borneo | Ended by the Bangkok Accord |
| 1963–1967 | National Liberation Front (NLF) and FLOSY | Aden | Britain withdraws; the NLF takes power |
| 1963–1976 | Dhofar Liberation Front, later PFLOAG | Oman | Defeated |
| 1965–1979 | ZANU and ZAPU against the Rhodesian state | Rhodesia | Majority rule and Zimbabwe |
| 1968–1998 | Republican and loyalist paramilitaries; the British Army | Northern Ireland | About 3,500 killed; the Good Friday Agreement |
| 1968–present | Chagossians | Chagos and Mauritius | Long legal campaign for return |
| 1982 | Argentina | Falkland Islands | Argentine defeat; sovereignty dispute continues |

## After the empire (1998 to today)

| Year | What happened |
|---|---|
| 1998 | Good Friday Agreement |
| 2002 | British Overseas Territories Act restores full British citizenship to most people in the territories |
| 2013 | UK government settles the Mau Mau claims: about £20 million for 5,228 Kenyans, with a statement of "sincere regret" |
| 2018 | Windrush scandal: Caribbean-born long-term residents wrongly detained or deported |
| 2019 | International Court of Justice advisory opinion says the separation of the Chagos Islands was unlawful; the UN General Assembly backs it |
| 2019 | Centenary of Amritsar; Theresa May calls it a "shameful scar" and expresses "deep regret", but no formal apology |
| 2021 | **Barbados becomes a republic** (30 November) |
| 2022 | Death of Elizabeth II (8 September); several museums begin returning Benin Bronzes to Nigeria |
| 2025 | UK and Mauritius sign a treaty (22 May) to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, with a long lease of Diego Garcia |
| 2026 | As of spring 2026, UK ratification of the Chagos treaty was reported shelved, with US opposition cited as a factor; Mauritius threatened legal action |

Britain still has **14 Overseas Territories**: Anguilla, Bermuda, the British Antarctic Territory, the British Indian Ocean Territory, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, the Falkland Islands, Gibraltar, Montserrat, the Pitcairn Islands, St Helena with Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia in Cyprus, and the Turks and Caicos Islands. Most of their inhabitants have chosen to remain British. The Commonwealth now has 56 members, including two (Mozambique and Rwanda) that were never British colonies, plus Gabon and Togo, which joined in 2022.

## When did the empire end?

There is no single answer. Common candidates:

- **1947**, because India was the centre of the empire and once it was gone the rest could not hold.
- **1956**, because Suez showed that Britain could no longer act as an independent great power.
- **1968–1971**, because the withdrawal from "East of Suez" ended Britain's world military role.
- **1997**, because Hong Kong was the last large, populous colony.
- **Not yet**, according to some critics, pointing to the Chagos dispute and the Overseas Territories.

## The whole series in one table: things that happened at the same time

This final table picks one overlap from each period. Each line is a reminder that the empire's story was happening alongside other big stories that we usually learn separately.

| Year | Something British | At the same time, elsewhere |
|---|---|---|
| 1600–1602 | East India Company chartered | Dutch VOC founded with far more capital; Tokugawa Japan about to begin |
| 1619–1620 | First enslaved Africans in Virginia; the Mayflower | Thirty Years' War starts in Europe |
| 1644–1649 | English Civil War; execution of Charles I | Ming dynasty falls to the Qing |
| 1686–1690 | EIC loses a war against the Mughals | Glorious Revolution in England |
| 1707 | Great Britain created | Aurangzeb dies; Mughal power starts to break up |
| 1739 | Maroon treaties in Jamaica; Stono Rebellion | Nadir Shah sacks Delhi |
| 1757 | Plassey | Qing China limits Western trade to Canton |
| 1770 | Bengal famine; Cook reaches Australia | Boston Massacre |
| 1775–1782 | American Revolution | First Anglo-Maratha War; Túpac Amaru II in Peru |
| 1788–1791 | First Fleet in Australia | French Revolution; Haitian Revolution begins |
| 1798 | Irish rising | Napoleon in Egypt |
| 1807 | British slave trade abolished | Sokoto Caliphate rising in West Africa |
| 1833–1834 | Slavery abolished in British colonies | Indian indentured labour to Mauritius begins |
| 1839–1842 | First Opium War; retreat from Kabul | Treaty of Waitangi |
| 1845–1849 | Irish Famine; Anglo-Sikh Wars | Revolutions of 1848 across Europe |
| 1857 | Indian Rebellion | Second Opium War; global financial panic |
| 1865 | Morant Bay, Jamaica | End of the American Civil War |
| 1867–1869 | Canadian Confederation; Suez Canal | Meiji Restoration |
| 1876–1878 | Victoria becomes Empress of India | Famine across India, China and Brazil |
| 1885 | Gordon dies; Indian National Congress founded; Riel hanged | Congo Free State created |
| 1896 | Anglo-Zanzibar War; First Chimurenga | Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa |
| 1899–1902 | Boer War and concentration camps | Philippine–American War; Boxer Rebellion |
| 1916 | Easter Rising; surrender at Kut | The Somme; Sykes–Picot |
| 1919 | Amritsar; Egyptian Revolution; Irish War of Independence | May Fourth in China; March First in Korea |
| 1930 | Salt March; Saya San rebellion | Great Depression |
| 1942–1943 | Fall of Singapore; Quit India; Bengal famine | Stalingrad; the Holocaust |
| 1947–1948 | Partition; end of the Palestine mandate; Windrush | Cold War begins; apartheid begins |
| 1952–1953 | Kenya Emergency; Iran coup; coronation | Korean War |
| 1956 | Suez | Hungarian Revolution |
| 1960 | Nigeria and Cyprus independent | French Africa's "Year of Africa" |
| 1965 | Rhodesia UDI; Chagos detached | Vietnam War escalates |
| 1982 | Falklands War | Israel invades Lebanon |
| 1997 | Hong Kong handover | Asian financial crisis begins the next day in Thailand |

## Thanks for reading

If you read all ten parts, you have seen about five centuries in one sweep. The aim was not to deliver a verdict on the empire, which historians still argue about, but to make it easier to see that events we learn in separate boxes, like "American history", "Indian history", "African history" or "Irish history", were often happening at the same time, and sometimes to the same people.
